inlaops registers six S3 methods against the `"bru"` class so that `vetiver_model()` works with inlabru fits out of the box — the same way it works with `lm()` or `mgcv::gam()`. This vignette walks through the full workflow: fitting, pinning, serving, and monitoring.

## Prerequisites

```{r}
library(inlabru)
library(vetiver)
library(pins)
library(plumber)
library(inlaops)
```

## 1. Fit a model

Always set `config = TRUE` so that the fit stores the posterior configurations needed for sampling at the `/predict` endpoint.

```{r}
set.seed(42)
n   <- 200
dat <- data.frame(
  x1 = rnorm(n),
  x2 = rnorm(n)
)
dat$y <- 2 + 0.8 * dat$x1 - 0.4 * dat$x2 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5)

fit <- bru(
  y ~ Intercept(1) + x1 + x2,
  family  = "gaussian",
  data    = dat,
  options = bru_options(
    control.compute = list(config = TRUE, dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE)
  )
)
```

## 2. Wrap with vetiver

`vetiver_model()` dispatches on the `"bru"` class. inlaops provides the
description, metadata, and input prototype automatically.

```{r}
v <- vetiver_model(fit, "gaussian_glm")
v
#> ── gaussian_glm ─ <bru> model for deployment
#> An inlabru model (gaussian family)
```

## 3. Store the prediction formula and model metrics as pin metadata

The prediction formula must be stored as a **character string** — R expressions
do not survive the YAML metadata round-trip. The handler parses it back with
`parse(text = ...)` at request time.

```{r}
v$metadata$user <- list(
  pred_formula = "~ Intercept + x1 + x2",
  n_samples    = 1000L,                  # default is 200; raise per pin if needed
  waic         = fit$waic$waic,
  dic          = fit$dic$dic
)
```

### Aside — parsnip-fitted models

If you fit via `parsnip::fit()` instead of `inlabru::bru()` directly, pass
the inner bru fit to `vetiver_model()`. This snippet is a stand-alone
alternative — the rest of the vignette continues with the bru-fitted `v`
from section 2:

```{r}
fit_p <- bru_reg(family = "gaussian") |>
  parsnip::set_engine("inlabru") |>
  parsnip::fit(y ~ Intercept(1) + x1 + x2, data = dat)

# Use a different name so this branch does not shadow the `v` we are about
# to pin and serve in section 4.
v_parsnip <- vetiver_model(fit_p$fit, "gaussian_glm")  # note: fit_p$fit
v_parsnip$metadata$user <- list(
  pred_formula = "~ Intercept + x1 + x2",
  n_samples    = 200L
)
```

The bridge does not auto-unwrap parsnip's `model_fit`. The unwrap is one
extra symbol; replicating all six S3 generics on the parsnip class would
be a lot of code for that.

## 4. Pin to a versioned board

```{r}
board <- board_temp()   # swap for board_s3(), board_connect(), etc.
vetiver_pin_write(board, v)

pin_versions(board, "gaussian_glm")
```

## 5. Test the endpoint locally

```{r}
pr() |>
  vetiver_api(v) |>
  pr_run(port = 8088)
```

In another R session (or with `httr2`):

```{r}
library(httr2)

new_obs <- data.frame(x1 = c(0.5, -1.2), x2 = c(1.0, 0.3))

resp <- request("http://127.0.0.1:8088/predict") |>
  req_body_raw(
    jsonlite::toJSON(new_obs, dataframe = "rows"),
    type = "application/json"
  ) |>
  req_perform()

resp_body_json(resp)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   .pred .pred_low .pred_high .pred_sd
#>   <dbl>     <dbl>      <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1  2.36      1.97       2.74    0.196
#> 2  1.08      0.70       1.46    0.193
```

The handler returns `.pred` (posterior mean), `.pred_low`/`.pred_high`
(2.5th/97.5th quantiles), and `.pred_sd` (posterior standard deviation).
This is a richer response than a point-estimate endpoint — downstream
consumers can propagate predictive uncertainty.

For packaging the model into a Docker container for production deployment, see
`vignette("docker")`.

### Verify the formula round-trip

The most likely point of failure is the formula serialisation. Confirm
explicitly that a character formula round-trips correctly before
deployment. We call `inlabru::generate()` directly here (rather than
`predict()`) to bypass any S3 dispatch surprises if you also have parsnip
loaded — `generate()` resolves unambiguously to inlabru's posterior
sampler regardless of search-path order:

```{r}
stopifnot(inherits(fit, "bru"))   # sanity check the right object

pred_str  <- "~ Intercept + x1 + x2"
pred_expr <- eval(parse(text = pred_str))

s1 <- inlabru::generate(fit, newdata = new_obs,
                        formula = ~ Intercept + x1 + x2, n.samples = 200)
s2 <- inlabru::generate(fit, newdata = new_obs,
                        formula = pred_expr, n.samples = 200)

# INLA uses its own internal RNG so s1 and s2 are independent draws from
# the same posterior — exact equality is neither expected nor meaningful.
# The check here is only that the parsed formula ran without error and
# returned the same shape of output.
stopifnot(identical(dim(s1), dim(s2)))
```

## 6. Track model quality across versions

INLA-specific fit metrics (WAIC, DIC) cannot be recomputed from a live
endpoint — they are only available at training time. Store them as pin metadata
and read them back per version for longitudinal monitoring:

```{r}
library(purrr)

versions <- pin_versions(board, "gaussian_glm")

map_dfr(versions$version, function(ver) {
  meta <- pin_meta(board, "gaussian_glm", version = ver)
  tibble::tibble(
    version = ver,
    waic    = meta$user$waic,
    dic     = meta$user$dic
  )
})
```

Standard prediction-drift monitoring uses `vetiver_compute_metrics()` against
the `.pred` column, the same as any other vetiver model. Drift monitoring
is time-windowed, so the input data needs a timestamp column. In a real
deployment this comes from the time you collected each observation — for
the vignette we synthesise one:

```{r}
monitoring_data <- dat  # in production: a holdout set collected since last deployment
monitoring_data$.pred <- inlabru::generate(
  fit, newdata = monitoring_data,
  formula = ~ Intercept + x1 + x2, n.samples = 500
) |> rowMeans()

# Synthetic timestamps for the example. Replace with real collection times.
monitoring_data$obs_date <- seq.Date(
  from       = as.Date("2026-01-01"),
  by         = "day",
  length.out = nrow(monitoring_data)
)

metrics_board <- board_temp()

new_metrics <- vetiver_compute_metrics(
  monitoring_data,
  date_var = obs_date,
  period   = "week",
  truth    = "y",
  estimate = ".pred"
)

# vetiver_pin_metrics() appends to an existing metrics pin — the first time
# you record metrics, write the pin directly with pins::pin_write(). On
# subsequent runs (e.g. weekly cron jobs), use vetiver_pin_metrics() so each
# new window's rows are appended without overwriting history.
if ("gaussian_glm_metrics" %in% pins::pin_list(metrics_board)) {
  vetiver_pin_metrics(metrics_board, new_metrics, "gaussian_glm_metrics")
} else {
  pins::pin_write(metrics_board, new_metrics, "gaussian_glm_metrics")
}

vetiver_plot_metrics(
  pins::pin_read(metrics_board, "gaussian_glm_metrics")
)
```

`period` is the rolling window — `"day"`, `"week"`, `"month"`, etc. Pick
the cadence that matches how often new observations arrive in production.

## Pins board options

| Board | Use case |
|---|---|
| `board_temp()` | Local development and testing |
| `board_s3()` | AWS-hosted teams |
| `board_azure()` | Azure-hosted teams |
| `board_connect()` | Posit Connect |

## Multi-likelihood models

`vetiver_ptype.bru()` extracts the input prototype from the **first**
likelihood's data slot. For models with multiple `bru_obs()` calls, supply
the prototype manually via `save_prototype` — vetiver accepts a tibble
there as a custom prototype, overriding the auto-derived one:

```{r}
v <- vetiver_model(
  fit,
  "multi_lhood_model",
  save_prototype = tibble::tibble(x1 = 0, x2 = 0)  # zero-row is fine
)
```
